screens.title: Filesystem hierarchy and the working directory
screens.narratorSegment: A Linux system presents a single hierarchical tree starting at the root, represented by slash. This structure places system files, user home directories, and mounted devices as branches beneath root. The working directory is the folder your terminal session is currently using; commands without explicit paths act relative to this location. The print working directory command reveals that exact path. For example, when you open a new shell you are usually placed in slash home slash yourusername. Running the print working directory command shows that full path and prevents mistakes like creating files in the wrong folder. One common misconception is that a new terminal always starts in root; it typically begins in the user home. Another is confusing the root user with the root directory; root is the privileged account and slash is the top of the filesystem. Practice with this definition: open a shell, run the print working directory command, then run a long listing to see the files surrounding you. Being precise about where you are avoids accidental file changes and helps you build correct relative paths later. What will you check with pwd before creating files?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Filesystem hierarchy
Core Concept

Root, home, and pwd

The tree starts at slash. Confirm exactly where you are with a single command.

Concrete example
Open a terminal. Run pwd. If it prints /home/yourusername you are in your home folder.
Misconception
A new terminal does not always start at root; it usually starts in your home directory. Check with pwd.
Key Takeaway
Always confirm your working directory before creating or deleting files to avoid affecting the wrong location.
Annotated example
$ pwd
/home/yourusername
$ ls -la
total 8
drwxr-xr-x 2 yourusername yourgroup 4096 Jan 1 12:00 .
Use these two commands together to orient and inspect your current directory contents before performing changes.

screens.title: Changing directories: cd, absolute vs relative paths
screens.narratorSegment: Changing directories is an everyday action and mastering both absolute and relative paths makes navigation fast and predictable. Use the cd command with an absolute path when you want to go to a fixed location from anywhere, for example cd slash var slash log takes you directly to that folder. When you work inside a project, relative paths save typing: from your project root cd src navigates into the src subfolder. Special tokens help: dot refers to the current directory, two dots refer to the parent, and tilde always expands to your home directory. A common practical sequence is: cd ~ to move home, mkdir -p projects/my_app/src to create a structure, then cd projects/my_app to work in the project root. A mistaken assumption is that cd without arguments always returns you to root — it returns you to your home. Also avoid ambiguous paths: if a folder name contains spaces, quote it. Practice these steps until the movement feels natural and predictable. Try a simple exercise: create a nested directory and navigate to it using both absolute and relative forms to reinforce the difference.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Changing directories
Process Flow

Absolute and relative cd

Step-by-step
  1. Run pwd to confirm your starting point.
  2. Use cd /full/path for absolute movement.
  3. Use cd relative/path for local moves.
  4. Use cd .. to go up one level, and cd ~ for home.
Common mistake
Assuming cd alone goes to root. It goes to your home directory. Confirm with pwd before continuing.
Concrete example and quick commands
# Start in your home
$ pwd
/home/yourusername
$ mkdir -p projects/my_app/src
$ cd projects/my_app
# Absolute path example
$ cd /var/log
# Back to home using tilde
$ cd ~
Try both the absolute and relative forms to build confidence. Quoted names are required when paths contain spaces.

screens.title: Listing contents with ls and interpreting ls -l
screens.narratorSegment: Listing directory contents is more than seeing filenames; it is how you inspect permissions, ownership, sizes, and timestamps. The ls command without options shows names. Add dash l for a long listing to see permission strings, link counts, owner, group, size, modification date, and the name. Add dash a to reveal hidden files that start with a dot. For instance ls dash la is a common combined form to get a comprehensive view. The first character in the ls dash l output indicates the file type: d for directory, dash for regular file, and l for symbolic link. The next nine characters indicate permissions in three groups: owner, group, and others, each with read, write, and execute markers. A frequent misconception is to ignore the first character or to misread the groups; practice reading rwxr-xr-- as owner rwx, group r-x, others r--. Use ls dash la regularly before permission changes or deletes so you know precisely what you are affecting. As an exercise, run ls dash la in a project folder and interpret each column to confirm ownership and access.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › ls and ls -l
Definition

Listing files with details

ls -l and ls -a reveal ownership, size, and hidden files so you can make informed changes.

Reading permission strings
Example: -rwxr-xr-- means owner has read, write, execute; group has read and execute; others have read only.
Common mistake
Don't confuse the file type character with permission bits. The first character indicates type, not permissions.
Command examples
$ ls
README.md  projects  scripts
$ ls -la
drwxr-xr-x 5 you you 4096 Jan 1 12:00 .
-rw-r--r-- 1 you you  123 Jan 1 11:58 README.md
Use ls -la to combine the long listing with hidden items. Interpret each column before changing files.

screens.title: Creating files and directories: touch and mkdir
screens.narratorSegment: Creating files and directories is the next practical skill. The touch command creates an empty file when the name does not exist and updates timestamps when it does. That makes touch useful for placeholders or build artifacts. To create directories, use mkdir with a name. When you need nested directories in one step, add the parent option with mkdir dash p; this creates any missing parents without error. For example mkdir dash p projects/my_app/src creates projects, my_app, and src if they don't exist. A common error is assuming mkdir will create parent folders by default; without -p it will fail if the parent does not exist. Another practical tip is to verify creation with ls -la immediately. Use touch README. md to add a project description and then inspect permissions; a new file may start with default permissions determined by your umask. As an exercise, create a project skeleton, add a README and a placeholder source file, then list the directory to confirm structure and timestamps. This sequence builds a predictable file layout for later steps. Creating files and directories: touch and mkdir means use touch for placeholder files and mkdir -p to create nested directories in one command. verify what you created with ls.. In practical terms, create empty files and nested directories reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Create files & directories
Process Flow

touch and mkdir -p

Quick commands
touch README.md creates a placeholder file. mkdir -p projects/my_app/src builds nested folders in one go.
Misconception
mkdir without -p will fail if parent folders are missing. Use -p for a single-step creation.
Concrete example
$ mkdir -p my_linux_project/src scripts docs
$ cd my_linux_project
$ touch README.md src/main.c

screens.title: Copying vs moving: cp and mv
screens.narratorSegment: Copying and moving are related but distinct operations. The cp command duplicates files or directories. For copying directories you must add the recursive option, cp dash r source_directory destination_directory. The mv command moves or renames files and directories; moving within the same filesystem is typically fast because only directory entries change. Use cp when you need a backup or to preserve the original, and mv when you want to reposition or rename a file. A common trap is using mv when you intended to preserve the source; another is forgetting -r with cp for directories, which results in an error. When copying, consider whether you need to preserve metadata like timestamps; some implementations offer a preserve option. As a concrete example, copy README. md into docs and rename it during the copy by supplying the new destination name. Then use mv to rename scripts/hello. sh to scripts/greet. sh. After each operation, run ls -la to confirm the intended effect. This comparison helps you choose the right command for backups, refactors, and reorganizations. Copying vs moving: cp and mv means cp duplicates data; mv renames or relocates. use cp -r for directories and mv for efficient renames or moves within the same filesystem.. In practical terms, understand when to duplicate and when to relocate files or directories. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Copying and moving
Comparison

When to copy and when to move

Use cp when
You need a duplicate or backup. For directories include -r to copy recursively.
Use mv when
You want to rename or relocate a file. It is efficient within the same filesystem.
Common mistake
Using mv when you intended to keep the original. When unsure, copy first then remove the original after verification.
Examples
# Copy a file into docs and rename
$ cp README.md docs/project_overview.md
# Copy a directory recursively
$ cp -r templates/ docs/templates_backup
# Move (rename) a script
$ mv scripts/hello.sh scripts/greet.sh
After each operation, use ls -la to verify the new and original locations so you avoid surprises.

screens.title: Deleting files and directories safely
screens.narratorSegment: Deleting files is irreversible in normal shell workflows, so apply caution. The rm command removes files. Use rmdir only for empty directories. To delete a directory and its contents you must use rm dash r to remove recursively, and adding dash f forces removal without prompts. The command rm dash rf slash is the infamous destructive instruction that attempts to delete everything from the root; never run this on a live system. Safer practices include using rm dash i to get interactive prompts, or listing files first with ls before removal. Another tactic is to move items to a temporary folder as a soft delete then remove them after verification. A common misconception is assuming deleted files go to a trash you can easily restore; in most command-line contexts they do not. For example to remove a directory named build safely, first run ls build to confirm contents, then rm -r build if you are certain. Incorporate verification steps into your deletion process to protect data integrity. Deleting files and directories safely means rm removes files permanently in normal workflows. use rmdir for empty directories and rm -i or verification steps to avoid mistakes.. In practical terms, use rm, rmdir, and safety options to avoid accidental data loss. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Safe deletion
Process Flow

rm, rmdir, and safe habits

Danger
Never run rm -rf / on a live system. It attempts to remove the entire filesystem hierarchy.
Safety checklist
1) List contents. 2) Use rm -i for interactive prompts. 3) Consider moving to a temp folder first.
Command examples
# Remove a single file with confirmation
$ rm -i notes.txt
# Remove an empty directory
$ rmdir old_folder
# Remove a directory recursively (use with care)
$ rm -r temp_build
If you must force removal, double-check the path and prefer to run rm -r on a non-critical test area first.

screens.title: File types in Linux
screens.narratorSegment: Files in Linux are categorized by type, and the type affects how you interact with them. The ls -l output uses the first character to show type: d denotes a directory, dash denotes a regular file, and l denotes a symbolic link that points to another file or directory. Symbolic links are lightweight pointers; removing the link does not remove the target unless you explicitly remove the target. Directories behave differently because execute permission on a directory allows entering and traversing it. A mistake learners sometimes make is treating a symbolic link as the actual file, which can lead to unexpected behavior when editing or deleting. When you see an l at the start of a listing, inspect the link target to ensure you understand what it references. Regular files include text, binaries, and many other formats. Recognizing these types helps you choose correct commands; for example, use rmdir only on empty directories and cp -r for directories. Try listing a folder with a mix of types and practice identifying each entry by its first character to build quick recognition.

Definition

Directory, file, link

Directory (d)

Regular file (-)
Text, binaries, or any non-directory entry.
Symbolic link (l)

screens.title: Permissions model: read, write, execute
screens.narratorSegment: File permissions in Linux determine who can read, write, or execute a file or directory. Permissions appear as a nine-character string split into three groups: owner, group, and others. Each group contains three markers: read, write, execute. Read allows viewing file contents; write permits modification; execute allows running a file as a program or, in directories, entering it. For directories the meaning shifts slightly: write allows creating and deleting entries, and execute allows traversing into them. Permissions are typically displayed along with owner and group names in the ls -l output. A classic misunderstanding is thinking execute always means runnable; for directories execute grants traversal, which is different from running a program. Practice interpreting rwxr-xr-- as owner all permissions, group read and execute, others read only. Understanding this mapping lets you protect files from unintended changes and expose only what is necessary. Try interpreting permissions on a few files to verify you can read owner, group, and others access without guessing. Permissions model: read, write, execute means permissions are grouped by owner, group, and others. each group has read, write, and execute bits that control specific capabilities.. In practical terms, how permission bits control owner, group, and others. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Permissions model
Core Concept

Read, write, execute explained

Permissions are shown as three sets: owner, group, others. Each set contains r, w, x.
For files: r = view, w = modify, x = run. For directories: r = list, w = create/delete, x = traverse.
Misconception: execute on a directory is not the same as executing a program. It allows you to enter that directory.
Practice interpret
-rwxr-xr-- 1 alice devs  256 Jan 1 12:00 program.sh
# owner: rwx (read, write, execute)
# group: r-x (read, execute)
# others: r-- (read only)
Interpreting strings like this helps you decide which chmod invocation is appropriate.

screens.title: Changing permissions with chmod (symbolic mode)
screens.narratorSegment: Symbolic mode with chmod is expressive and readable. You specify who (u for user/owner, g for group, o for others, a for all), the operation (+ to add, - to remove, = to set exactly), and the permission letters (r, w, x). For instance chmod u+x script. sh adds execute permission for the owner only, which is a common step after creating a shell script. chmod o-w file. txt removes write access for others. Using symbolic mode is convenient when you want to change a single class without touching the others. A typical misconception is thinking chmod u+x changes group or others; it affects only the user unless you include other classes. Combine multiple operations with commas, for example chmod u=rw,g=r,o=r file. txt sets specific access explicitly. After each chmod, verify the change with ls -l to confirm the bits changed as expected. Symbolic mode is particularly helpful in iterative workflows where you add or remove individual permissions while retaining the rest of the configuration. Changing permissions with chmod (symbolic mode) means chown uses letters and operators to adjust permission bits precisely. use u, g, o, a with +, -, = to modify specific classes.. In practical terms, use u, g, o, a with +, -, = to add, remove, or set bits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › chmod (symbolic)
Process

Symbolic mode examples

Add execute for owner
chmod u+x scripts/hello.sh then verify with ls -l.
Remove write for others
chmod o-w notes.txt keeps others from modifying the file.
Concrete commands
# Make script executable for owner
$ chmod u+x scripts/hello.sh
# Remove write for others
$ chmod o-w README.md
# Set exact permissions: user rw, group r, others r
$ chmod u=rw,g=r,o=r file.txt
Use ls -l after each change. Symbolic mode is precise and avoids altering unrelated classes accidentally.

screens.title: Changing permissions with chmod (octal mode)
screens.narratorSegment: Octal mode offers a compact way to set permissions by using three digits. Each digit represents the sum of read as four, write as two, and execute as one for owner, group, and others respectively. For example 7 equals 4 plus 2 plus 1, meaning read, write, execute. A common pattern is chmod 755 which sets owner to read, write, execute and group and others to read and execute; this is typical for executable scripts and directories that should be readable by others. Another frequent example is chmod 644 for regular files, which gives the owner read and write and others read only. Octal mode is efficient when you want to set all three classes explicitly in a single command. A mistake learners sometimes make is using the wrong digit order — remember it is owner, group, then others. After applying an octal change, verify the result with ls -l and, if needed, use symbolic mode to tweak individual bits. Practice converting common strings to octal values to build fluency. Changing permissions with chmod (octal mode) means octal digits encode read=4, write=2, execute=1 for owner, group, and others. use three digits like 755 or 644 to set permissions concisely.. In practical terms, use numeric codes for concise permission settings (e.g., 755, 644). A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › chmod (octal)
Code Walkthrough

Octal values explained

Map r=4, w=2, x=1 and sum for each class in owner, group, others order.
Example: 7 (rwx), 5 (r-x), 4 (r--). So 754 means owner rwx, group r-x, others r--.
Misconception: the digits are owner→group→others, not alphabetical or some other order. Keep the order straight.
Examples and verification
# Typical script permission
$ chmod 755 scripts/hello.sh
# Typical regular file
$ chmod 644 README.md
# Set owner rwx, group r-x, others r--
$ chmod 754 scripts/hello.sh
$ ls -l scripts/hello.sh
After using octal mode, confirm with ls -l. Use symbolic mode to adjust one class if you changed more than intended.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: These are the essential concepts to retain. First, the filesystem is a single tree with root at slash; always confirm your current directory before making changes. Second, practice safe file manipulation: create with touch and mkdir -p, copy with cp -r, move or rename with mv, and delete only after verification. Third, file types and permissions matter: the first character in a long listing indicates type and the three permission groups show who can read, write, or execute. Use chmod in symbolic mode to adjust individual bits or octal mode for concise changes. Finally, adopt safe habits such as using rm -i, verifying with ls -la, and avoiding destructive recursive operations on critical paths. Keep these practices in mind as you build and maintain projects on Linux. They will reduce mistakes and improve the security of your files.

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter you will learn the core skills needed to manage files and directories on a Linux system. We begin by locating where you are with the print working directory command and then move through navigation using absolute and relative paths. You will practice creating files and directories, copying and moving content, and safely removing items while learning the conventions that prevent accidental data loss. A large section is dedicated to file permissions: you will see how read, write, and execute bits control access and how to change permissions using both symbolic and octal modes. These skills matter because every administrative task depends on correct file placement and access controls. For example, making a script executable or preventing world write access can be the difference between a working tool and a security risk. As you progress, notice common mistakes like deleting without checking or setting overly permissive modes. By the end you will be able to set up a small project directory, verify its contents, and protect files using proper permissions. Ready to explore the commands and patterns that make Linux file management reliable?

These objectives map to practical skills you will practice. First, you will navigate the Linux file system using both absolute and relative paths so you can reliably move to the right folders. For example, using an absolute path like slash home slash yourname reaches the same target from anywhere, whereas a relative path moves you from your current location. Second, you will create, copy, move, and delete files and directories from the command line. That includes using mkdir with the parent option, touch for new files, cp and mv for duplication and renaming, and cautious use of rm and rmdir. Third, you will understand and modify file and directory permissions with both symbolic notation and octal numbers. You will learn the meaning of read, write, and execute bits and practice chmod commands to set safe access. Finally, you will identify common file types found in Linux and apply best practices for organizing projects and protecting data. Each objective focuses on hands-on use so you leave with muscle memory, not just theory.

This page extends the objectives with practical checks you can perform in a terminal. First, you will verify your location with print working directory and confirm contents with a long listing. This checks that you know where you start. Second, you will create nested directories with mkdir dash p and populate them with placeholder files using touch and simple redirection. A concrete practice: create a project folder with src, scripts, and docs and verify the structure with ls dash la. Third, you will practice safe deletion and recovery-aware habits: prefer rmdir for empty folders, use rm dash i when removing multiple files, and never run recursive force removal on the root. Finally, you will learn to interpret file type indicators such as d for directory, dash for regular file, l for symbolic link, and use that understanding to avoid permission and path errors. These practice-focused objectives are designed to leave you confident running each command and verifying results immediately.

A Linux system presents a single hierarchical tree starting at the root, represented by slash. This structure places system files, user home directories, and mounted devices as branches beneath root. The working directory is the folder your terminal session is currently using; commands without explicit paths act relative to this location. The print working directory command reveals that exact path. For example, when you open a new shell you are usually placed in slash home slash yourusername. Running the print working directory command shows that full path and prevents mistakes like creating files in the wrong folder. One common misconception is that a new terminal always starts in root; it typically begins in the user home. Another is confusing the root user with the root directory; root is the privileged account and slash is the top of the filesystem. Practice with this definition: open a shell, run the print working directory command, then run a long listing to see the files surrounding you. Being precise about where you are avoids accidental file changes and helps you build correct relative paths later. What will you check with pwd before creating files?

Changing directories is an everyday action and mastering both absolute and relative paths makes navigation fast and predictable. Use the cd command with an absolute path when you want to go to a fixed location from anywhere, for example cd slash var slash log takes you directly to that folder. When you work inside a project, relative paths save typing: from your project root cd src navigates into the src subfolder. Special tokens help: dot refers to the current directory, two dots refer to the parent, and tilde always expands to your home directory. A common practical sequence is: cd ~ to move home, mkdir -p projects/my_app/src to create a structure, then cd projects/my_app to work in the project root. A mistaken assumption is that cd without arguments always returns you to root — it returns you to your home. Also avoid ambiguous paths: if a folder name contains spaces, quote it. Practice these steps until the movement feels natural and predictable. Try a simple exercise: create a nested directory and navigate to it using both absolute and relative forms to reinforce the difference.

Listing directory contents is more than seeing filenames; it is how you inspect permissions, ownership, sizes, and timestamps. The ls command without options shows names. Add dash l for a long listing to see permission strings, link counts, owner, group, size, modification date, and the name. Add dash a to reveal hidden files that start with a dot. For instance ls dash la is a common combined form to get a comprehensive view. The first character in the ls dash l output indicates the file type: d for directory, dash for regular file, and l for symbolic link. The next nine characters indicate permissions in three groups: owner, group, and others, each with read, write, and execute markers. A frequent misconception is to ignore the first character or to misread the groups; practice reading rwxr-xr-- as owner rwx, group r-x, others r--. Use ls dash la regularly before permission changes or deletes so you know precisely what you are affecting. As an exercise, run ls dash la in a project folder and interpret each column to confirm ownership and access.

Creating files and directories is the next practical skill. The touch command creates an empty file when the name does not exist and updates timestamps when it does. That makes touch useful for placeholders or build artifacts. To create directories, use mkdir with a name. When you need nested directories in one step, add the parent option with mkdir dash p; this creates any missing parents without error. For example mkdir dash p projects/my_app/src creates projects, my_app, and src if they don't exist. A common error is assuming mkdir will create parent folders by default; without -p it will fail if the parent does not exist. Another practical tip is to verify creation with ls -la immediately. Use touch README. md to add a project description and then inspect permissions; a new file may start with default permissions determined by your umask. As an exercise, create a project skeleton, add a README and a placeholder source file, then list the directory to confirm structure and timestamps. This sequence builds a predictable file layout for later steps. Creating files and directories: touch and mkdir means use touch for placeholder files and mkdir -p to create nested directories in one command. verify what you created with ls.. In practical terms, create empty files and nested directories reliably. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Copying and moving are related but distinct operations. The cp command duplicates files or directories. For copying directories you must add the recursive option, cp dash r source_directory destination_directory. The mv command moves or renames files and directories; moving within the same filesystem is typically fast because only directory entries change. Use cp when you need a backup or to preserve the original, and mv when you want to reposition or rename a file. A common trap is using mv when you intended to preserve the source; another is forgetting -r with cp for directories, which results in an error. When copying, consider whether you need to preserve metadata like timestamps; some implementations offer a preserve option. As a concrete example, copy README. md into docs and rename it during the copy by supplying the new destination name. Then use mv to rename scripts/hello. sh to scripts/greet. sh. After each operation, run ls -la to confirm the intended effect. This comparison helps you choose the right command for backups, refactors, and reorganizations. In practical terms, understand when to duplicate and when to relocate files or directories. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Deleting files is irreversible in normal shell workflows, so apply caution. The rm command removes files. Use rmdir only for empty directories. To delete a directory and its contents you must use rm dash r to remove recursively, and adding dash f forces removal without prompts. The command rm dash rf slash is the infamous destructive instruction that attempts to delete everything from the root; never run this on a live system. Safer practices include using rm dash i to get interactive prompts, or listing files first with ls before removal. Another tactic is to move items to a temporary folder as a soft delete then remove them after verification. A common misconception is assuming deleted files go to a trash you can easily restore; in most command-line contexts they do not. For example to remove a directory named build safely, first run ls build to confirm contents, then rm -r build if you are certain. Incorporate verification steps into your deletion process to protect data integrity. The ls -l output uses the first character to show type: d denotes a directory, dash denotes a regular file, and l denotes a symbolic link that points to another file or directory.
